title: Mass, Weight and Gravity
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Physics
summary: Mass is how much matter an object has (kg); weight is the pull of gravity on it (N). Learn the difference, how to measure each, and why your weight would change on the Moon but your mass would not.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Describe the difference between mass, measured in kilograms (kg), and weight, measured in newtons (N). (6Pf.01)
Describe what gravity does: when gravity changes (for example on the Moon), an object's weight changes but its mass stays the same. (6Pf.02)

blocks.text: 2. Mass

**Mass** is the amount of matter in an object — how much "stuff" it is made of. A brick has more mass than a sponge of the same size because it has more matter packed into it. Mass is measured in **kilograms (kg)** or **grams (g)** using a **balance**. Mass does **not** depend on where the object is: a 2 kg bag of rice has a mass of 2 kg in Cairo, on top of a mountain, on the Moon or in space.
3. Weight

**Weight** is a **force**: it is the pull of **gravity** on an object's mass. Because it is a force, weight is measured in **newtons (N)** using a **forcemeter** (also called a newton meter). Weight always acts **towards the centre of the planet** — we call this direction "downwards".

blocks.text: 4. How to use a forcemeter accurately

items: Choose a forcemeter with a suitable range: a 0–10 N forcemeter for a pencil case, a 0–50 N forcemeter for a bag of books. If the object is too heavy, the spring can be damaged.
Hold the forcemeter **vertically** (straight up and down) by its top ring, with nothing hanging on it, and check that the pointer is on **0**. If it is not, adjust it to zero first.
Hang the object gently on the hook and wait until it **stops moving**.
Read the scale with your eye **level** with the pointer. Work out what each small division is worth (for example, 2 divisions per newton means each division is 0.5 N).
Repeat the reading two or three times; if one reading is very different, check it again.

blocks.text: 5. Gravity

items: **Gravity** is a force that pulls objects towards each other. It is a **non-contact** force: it works without touching.
Every object with mass has gravity, but it is only strong enough to notice for huge objects such as planets, moons and stars.

A planet with **more mass** usually has **stronger gravity**. Jupiter has much more mass than the Earth, so its gravity is stronger; the Moon has much less mass than the Earth, so its gravity is weaker.
Gravity gets **weaker** the further you go from the planet. Far out in space, away from planets and stars, an object's weight is almost zero — but its mass is still the same.

blocks.text: 6. Working out weight

The strength of gravity is given in **newtons per kilogram (N/kg)** — the number of newtons of weight for each kilogram of mass. On Earth gravity is about **10 N/kg**, so every 1 kg has a weight of about 10 N.

blocks.title: The rule
blocks.text:
**weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravity (N/kg)**
To find the mass from a weight on Earth: **mass (kg) = weight (N) ÷ 10**. Always change grams into kilograms first (500 g = 0.5 kg).

rows: Deep space, far from any planet

blocks.text: Look down the columns: the **weight changes** from place to place because the **gravity changes**, but the **mass is the same** in every row. This is the key idea of this topic. (Scientists use 9.8 N/kg for the Earth; a question will tell you which value to use; this course uses 10 N/kg.)

**Why can astronauts jump so high on the Moon?** Their mass is the same, but the Moon's gravity is about one sixth of the Earth's, so their weight is much smaller. The pull back down is weaker, so they can jump higher and carry heavy backpacks easily.

blocks.alt: The full Moon showing grey craters and dark plains
blocks.caption: The Moon has much less mass than the Earth, so its gravity is only about one sixth as strong: an astronaut's weight is smaller there, but her mass is the same.
blocks.credit: Photo: Gregory H. Revera / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

blocks.title: Everyday words vs science words
blocks.text: People say "I weigh 40 kg" and bathroom scales show kilograms. In science this is your **mass**. Your **weight** is a force: 40 kg × 10 N/kg = **400 N**. In a Checkpoint answer, a weight must be given in **N**, and a mass in **kg** or **g**.

blocks.title: القاعدة الذهبية
blocks.text: الكتلة (mass) = كمية المادة في الجسم، وحدتها الكيلوجرام kg، تُقاس بالميزان، ولا تتغير أبداً في أي مكان. الوزن (weight) = قوة جذب الجاذبية للجسم، وحدته النيوتن N، يُقاس بالميزان الزنبركي، ويتغير لو تغيرت الجاذبية. على القمر: الكتلة نفسها، لكن الوزن أقل. على الأرض: الوزن = الكتلة × 10.
7. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Complete the table. [2 marks]  Quantity: mass / weight. Unit: ? Measuring instrument: ?

items: Mass: unit **kilogram (kg)** (or g); measured with a **balance**.
Weight: unit **newton (N)**; measured with a **forcemeter**.
(1 mark for each correct row.) **Common mistake:** writing "kg" for weight.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — A bag of potatoes has a mass of 3 kg. Gravity on Earth is 10 N/kg. Calculate the weight of the bag on Earth. [1 mark]

items: weight = mass × gravity = 3 × 10 = **30 N**.
Give the unit N — "30" alone may not get the mark if the unit is asked for.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg on Earth. Gravity on the Moon is 1.6 N/kg. (a) What is her mass on the Moon? [1] (b) Calculate her weight on the Moon. [1] (c) Explain why her weight changes but her mass does not. [2]

items: (a) **80 kg** — mass does not change.
(b) 80 × 1.6 = **128 N**. (Check: on Earth she weighs 800 N; 128 N is much less, which makes sense.)
(c) Mass is the amount of matter in her body, and this does not change when she moves (1). Weight is the pull of gravity; the Moon's gravity is weaker than the Earth's, so her weight is smaller (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A pencil case hangs on a forcemeter on Earth. The forcemeter reads 4.5 N. (a) What is the weight of the pencil case? [1] (b) Calculate its mass in grams. Use 10 N/kg. [2]

items: (a) The forcemeter measures weight directly: **4.5 N**.
(b) mass = weight ÷ gravity = 4.5 ÷ 10 = 0.45 kg (1). Change to grams: 0.45 × 1000 = **450 g** (1).
**Common mistake:** writing 45 g (forgetting that 1 kg = 1000 g).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Malak says: "If I take my 1 kg box of dates to the Moon, it will become lighter, so there will be fewer dates in it." Is she right? Explain. [2 marks]

items: No (1). Its **weight** will be less because the Moon's gravity is weaker, but its **mass** (the amount of matter — the number of dates) stays the same: 1 kg (1).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Giving weight in kg or mass in N. Weight → N; mass → kg or g.
Saying "mass changes on the Moon". Mass never changes when you move to another place.
Saying "there is no gravity on the Moon". The Moon has gravity — it is weaker than the Earth's (that is why astronauts land back on the surface after jumping).
Saying gravity pulls "down" without understanding that down means towards the centre of the planet.
Forgetting to change grams to kilograms before multiplying by 10 (200 g = 0.2 kg → 2 N, not 2000 N).
Using a balance to measure weight in an answer about instruments: a forcemeter measures weight.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Match / complete a table** of quantity, unit and instrument.
**Read a forcemeter** — find what each small division is worth (often 0.5 N) before reading.
**Calculate** weight = mass × gravity (use the value of gravity given in the question). Show the multiplication and write N.
**Moon/planet questions** — "What happens to the mass? What happens to the weight?" Answer both separately: mass stays the same; weight goes down (or up on a bigger planet).
**Explain** — for 2 marks say what mass is AND what weight depends on (gravity).
**Read a bar chart** of weights in different places and say why they differ.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Mass, weight and gravity — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Use gravity on Earth = 10 N/kg unless the question gives another value. For longer answers write yours on paper, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: Which unit is used for weight?
questions.e: Weight is a force, and forces are measured in newtons (N). Kilograms and grams are units of mass.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure weight?
questions.e: A forcemeter (newton meter) measures forces, including weight, in N. A balance measures mass.

questions.q: A box has a mass of 6 kg. Gravity on Earth is 10 N/kg. What is the weight of the box on Earth?
What is the name of the force that pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth?
questions.e: Gravity. The pull of gravity on an object is its weight.

questions.p:
Question 7
An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. She travels to the Moon, where gravity is 1.6 N/kg.
questions.q: (a) What is her mass on the Moon?
questions.e: Mass does not change from place to place: 60 kg.

questions.p:
Question 7
An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. She travels to the Moon, where gravity is 1.6 N/kg.
questions.q: (b) Calculate her weight on the Moon.
questions.e: weight = mass × gravity = 60 × 1.6 = 96 N. (On Earth she weighs 60 × 10 = 600 N.)

questions.p:
Question 7
An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. She travels to the Moon, where gravity is 1.6 N/kg.
questions.q: (c) Explain why her weight on the Moon is different from her weight on Earth, but her mass is the same.
questions.ms: 1 mark: mass is the amount of matter (in her body), which does not change (when she moves). 1 mark: weight is the pull/force of gravity, and gravity on the Moon is weaker (than on Earth), so her weight is less. Do not accept: there is no gravity on the Moon.
questions.e: Her mass is the amount of matter in her body, and that does not change when she travels. Her weight is the force of gravity pulling on her; the Moon's gravity (1.6 N/kg) is weaker than the Earth's (10 N/kg), so her weight is smaller.

c: Weight is the amount of matter in an object.
An object's mass is smaller on the Moon.
Mass and weight are the same thing.
Weight is a force, measured in newtons.
questions.e: Weight is the force of gravity on an object, measured in N. The amount of matter is mass, which stays the same on the Moon. Mass and weight are different quantities with different units.

questions.q: (b) Use the weight of the rock on Earth to find the mass of the rock. Gravity on Earth is 10 N/kg.
questions.e: From the chart, the rock weighs 40 N on Earth. mass = weight ÷ gravity = 40 ÷ 10 = 4 kg. Its mass is 4 kg in all four places.

questions.q: A stone has a weight of 50 N on Earth. It is taken to the Moon. What will its weight be on the Moon?
questions.e: The Moon's gravity is weaker than the Earth's, so the weight is less than 50 N (5 kg × 1.6 N/kg = 8 N). It is not 0 N because the Moon does have gravity.

questions.q: Laila says: "My weight is 35 kg." Explain what is wrong with her statement and write a correct version. (Gravity on Earth = 10 N/kg.)
questions.ms: 1 mark: kg is the unit of mass, not weight / weight is a force so it is measured in newtons. 1 mark: correct statement, e.g. "My mass is 35 kg" OR "My weight is 350 N". Accept either.
questions.e: Kilograms measure mass, but weight is a force, measured in newtons. Correct versions: "My mass is 35 kg" or "My weight is 350 N" (35 × 10 = 350).

blocks.title: Remember
items: Mass = amount of matter; kg or g; measured with a balance; the same everywhere.
Weight = force of gravity on an object; newtons (N); measured with a forcemeter; acts towards the centre of the planet.
Weight = mass × gravity. On Earth, about 10 N for every 1 kg.
Weaker gravity (the Moon) → less weight; stronger gravity (Jupiter) → more weight; the mass never changes.
Change grams into kilograms before working out weight.
